title: Market Day: thirty seconds at the table, three rounds after it
summary: A thirty second pitch delivered live to strangers at the stand, then the full format against a parent on whether selling to your own people counts as a test, judged on the real ballot, and the Sprout's shop-day card run by them.
materials: the sand timers, two minute and one minute, and the call bell
a blank ballot for the judging parent, and a second one for you to self-score
your closing numbers from the stand: what sold, the takings, and the gap if there was one
a parent to debate and a second parent or grown-up to judge
this week's Sprout parent card, three coins and paper and crayons, for the teach-someone-younger quest

steps.title: Two kinds of speaking in one day
steps.body:
Today you speak twice and the two could not be less alike.

The first is thirty seconds long, delivered standing up, to people who did not come to listen to you. That is the barker's job and it is the hardest short speech there is, because your audience is walking and you get one shot at making them stop. It happens at the table, during Market Day, and the step below is how you build it.

The second is the full round against a parent, all the speeches you have learned this season in their proper order, judged on a real ballot by somebody who is not debating. That happens after the table comes down, when your hands still smell of coins.

The motion: selling to friends and family is not a real test of a shop.

That motion is aimed straight at the afternoon you just had, on purpose, and you may take either side of it honestly. If you argue for it, you have the strongest evidence in the room: people who love you bought from you, and love is not a market. If you argue against it, you have evidence too, and it is just as real: they handed over money they could have kept, somebody walked away without buying, and you had to make change in front of a queue like anyone else. Pick the side you actually lean towards and let the parent take the other. If you both lean the same way, the parent argues the far side anyway.

Use today's numbers as evidence, not as feelings. How many came. How many bought. How many walked. What the one thing that broke was. A claim with a number attached to it beats a claim with a sigh attached to it, and this is the first debate all season where the evidence is yours and nobody else in the world has it.

The judge writes on the ballot while you speak and reads the result out loud at the end, whichever way it went. You self-score a second ballot at the same time. Comparing the two afterwards is the point: not who won, but where the two ballots disagreed about why.

steps.title: The barker's thirty seconds
steps.body:
Write this before the table goes out, and say it out loud at least three times before anybody arrives, because a pitch read off a card is not a pitch.

Thirty seconds holds four things and no more. What it is, in one plain sentence a stranger could repeat to somebody else without you there. Who it is for, said as a person and not as everyone. What it costs, said straight out with no apology in your voice; the price is a fact, not a confession. And one reason to stop walking, which is the only sentence in the whole thing that has to be interesting.

Write it, then cut it. Almost every first draft is fifty seconds pretending to be thirty. Read it aloud against the one minute timer and cut whatever you had to rush. The words you cut are the ones you did not need.

Two voice rules for a table. Speak to the far side of the path, not to the person in front of you, or the third person along will never hear you. And stop talking when you have finished, all the way, and let the silence sit. A barker who keeps going after the pitch has ended talks people back out of stopping.

Deliver it live at the stand. Not once: every time a new person comes near enough to hear it. It will feel odd the first time and ordinary by the fourth, and the fourth one will be your best.
checklist: It is written down and it holds all four things: what it is, who it is for, what it costs, and one reason to stop
It was timed against the one minute timer and cut until it fitted inside thirty seconds
I said it out loud three times before the first customer arrived
I said it to every new person who came near the table, not just the first one
I said the price without apologising for it, every single time

steps.title: Teach someone younger
steps.body:
They were your first customer. Now you run their card.

A parent card is the short card in the app that a grown-up normally does with Sprout. This week it is yours, and it is the one built around your own counter: they choose one thing from your table, count three coins into your hand, and then draw what they bought.

Read the card all the way through before Market Day starts, because part of it has to happen at the stand and the rest happens afterwards with paper and crayons. Set the sale up in advance with a grown-up so it cannot fail: three coins in their purse, put there by the grown-up and not taken out of your float, and whatever they choose costs three coins today. Their money has to come from outside your shop, or the three coins you take tonight are three coins you already had. They are young, and their first sale is not the place to meet a price they cannot pay.

At the table, do the hard thing: wait. Let them put the coins into your hand one at a time and say the numbers themselves, however slowly, even with a queue behind them. Do not count for them, do not finish their counting, do not take the coins out of their hand. If they lose their place, hold your hand still and let them start again.

Then afterwards, the drawing. They draw what they bought and tell you about it, and your only job is to ask and wait. Ask them how many coins they gave you. Ask them what they would buy next time.

Watch for one thing that surprises you: a number they land on without counting, or something they noticed about your shop that you had stopped seeing.
checklist: I read the card all the way through before the stand opened
The sale was set up in advance so their three coins were exactly enough
They counted the coins into my hand themselves, one at a time, out loud, with nobody counting for them
I waited for them even with people waiting behind them
They drew what they bought and I asked and waited instead of telling

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record two things. First, one live delivery of the thirty second pitch at the table, with a real person walking up, if a camera can be left standing somewhere polite. Second, round three of the debate: both closings, whole face in frame, and the judge reading the ballot out loud. Then keep rolling for one honest sentence: which of your opponent's arguments was strongest, and what today's numbers would have to look like before you changed your own mind.
